title: Looking for honest feedback
author: jildos_legoplanet
selftext:
Hi everyone,

I’m exploring a game concept and I’d really appreciate brutally honest feedback before I invest more time into building it.

The core idea is based on **Rock Paper Scissors Lizard Spock**, but instead of being pure luck, the game is designed around psychology and pattern recognition.

Here’s the concept:

* Every round, both players secretly choose one of the five symbols.
* You can see your opponent’s previous choices and outcomes.
* The goal is to recognize habits, adapt, and outthink your opponent.
* There are **no power-ups, no randomness modifiers, no hidden stats**. The game intentionally avoids giving players artificial advantages.
* Winning should come from reading people better, not grinding or spending money.

The ambition is to make something that’s:

* easy to learn in seconds,
* difficult to master,
* quick to play (30–60 seconds),
* and satisfying because victories feel earned.

One thing I’m experimenting with is adding small cinematic moments after each round (e.g. “Spock vaporizes Rock”) to make every win feel impactful without slowing the game down.

**My biggest concern**

Will this actually remain interesting after dozens or hundreds of matches?

Is there enough depth in trying to read another person, or would it eventually feel repetitive because the underlying mechanics are still RPSLS?

**Questions**

* Would you play something like this?
* What do you think would become boring first?
* Where do you think the design would break down?
* Is there another game that already solved this problem well?
* If you had to kill this idea, what argument would you use?

Please don’t worry about hurting my feelings—I’m specifically looking for reasons **not** to build this.

Thanks!

comments.author: Blizzxx
comments.body:
So it's just rock paper scissors with 2 more options? I mean...how boring does rock paper scissors get to you in person? Pretty fast for me. Adding 2 more to the mix also breaks the triangle counter system of how RPS works as a whole. You should try playing your game in person with others first to ensure it actually has charm because right now it feels like a $1 idea. 

Additionally I think you've really tunnel visioned on your idea of psychology based strategy utilizing an opponent's prior history. What stops the player from just picking randomly? What does it even matter? 

Lastly, realistically do you genuinely see yourself playing hundreds of matches of Rock Paper Scissor? I'd love to know how many times you think you've played it IRL, it's certainly much less than that.

replies.author: jildos_legoplanet
replies.body:
Thanks for the feedback! Generally, the most simple games are the most addicting for the masses. It is intended to be a $1 game (or free even with analytics add-on as premium)

The younger generation around me seem to have made RPS super popular again, using it for almost anything nowadays. Perhaps there should be a physical form of using it with your friends

comments.author: yanenrogne
comments.body: I think the idea of psychology is good, but the RPS delivery format is the weak link, consider something novel!

comments.author: anotherlebowski
comments.body:
I understand your thought process that you don't want to add power ups/modifiers because it makes the game more RNG oriented, and you want it to be purely skill oriented so you can lean into the psychology element.

Here's my concern - the remaining game becomes extremely bare bones.  It's essentially just rock paper scissors with five options, encouraging the player to think harder than they normally would in a game of rock paper scissors.  

I would challenge the idea that power ups/modifiers always contribute to randomness over skill.  I'm a believer that a little bit of randomness actually makes the game more skill oriented because it forces you to play differently each time, as opposed to defaulting to your favorite strategy.  

That said, I mostly develop PVE Roguelike style games, so battling against random encounters is part of it. In PVP, you're always playing a different person, and that inherently brings some level of variation to every match.  

I still think your game needs one more axis of variation to differentiate it from existing rock paper scissors.  Your premise is "not based on luck." You need some mechanic that leans into that.  Right now that mechanic seems to be your ability to view the history of moves.  Is that enough?

replies.author: jildos_legoplanet
replies.body:
Thanks, this is probably the most useful piece of feedback I’ve received.
I actually agree with your core point: if the game ends up being “just RPSLS with history,” then it probably isn’t interesting enough.
The hypothesis I’m trying to validate is that the game eventually stops being about choosing symbols and starts being about reading people. The move history is just one way to support that—it isn’t meant to be the mechanic itself.
I also agree that the game may need a second axis of variation. My hesitation is that I don’t want to add mechanics just for the sake of complexity or randomness. If there is another axis, I’d prefer it to deepen the psychological aspect rather than distract from it.
At this stage I’m trying to answer one question: after 50 or 100 matches, are players thinking “Which symbol should I pick?” or “I think I understand how this person plays.” If it’s the former, the concept probably doesn’t work. If it’s the latter, then there may be something worth building.
I like this response because it does three things:

It validates their criticism rather than dismissing it.
It shows you’re testing a hypothesis instead of defending a finished design.
It subtly demonstrates that you’re thinking at a systems level, which tends to earn respect in game development communities.

I would avoid mentioning potential solutions like behavioral profiles, analytics, or hidden habits in the reply. Those are possible implementations, but they’re also ideas you’d probably rather explore yourself first. Keep the discussion centered on the design question rather than revealing all of your potential answers.

replies.author: Interesting-Yam23
replies.body:
\> The hypothesis I’m trying to validate is that the game eventually stops being about choosing symbols and starts being about reading people.

That's what every multiplayer game eventually is. Fighting games require a lot of skill and technique and execution, but at the high level it's often "What is my opponent going to do"?

I think you're operating under the assumption that complexity removes or obfuscates the psychology element. But RPS with 5 choices instead of 3 is just is a simple game that would get old in minutes. Every fun multiplayer game, complexity at whatever level it's at, has a deep psychology element. 

\> I would avoid mentioning potential solutions like behavioral profiles, analytics, or hidden habits in the reply.

Did you forget to read the comment you had AI write for you? And, I disagree. You have to mention specific solutions. As far as I know your game is literally RPS with 5 choices. What else? That's a game you play test in 5 mins with a few friends. Have you done that? Do they enjoy it?

comments.author: FoxForgeDev
comments.body: None of your concept ideas are different than the current version of RPS (except 5 symbols instead of 3 - which might break the game). If people play RSP for multiple rounds they are already trying to recognize opponents patterns and counter.

replies.author: jildos_legoplanet
replies.body: Thanks, and that is the whole point of investigating this concept. The hypothesis is that this not a game of luck but of genuine skill. Therefore there is an incentive to get better at the game. Combining this with a (relative) progression and ranking system, the theory is that people will remain engaged to this. Think of flappy bird from 10 years ago.

comments.author: Jolly-Rip5973
comments.body:
I don't think I would like that. I think it would frustrating. A good player would wipe the floor with most players. 

1 out of 5 players would completely dominate the game and that means 4 out 5 players would end up being frustrated and quit. 

You would also need rewards to motivate people to keep playing but if you have no level ups or no buffs, there is nothing to earn except maybe a title. 

The problem with titles is that if you have a top 50 leaderboard, it doesn't scale well when you start getting player based bigger than 500 players. 

You need a game with defined goals, built incentives to get players to play and keep playing.

comments.author: jildos_legoplanet
comments.body:
Thanks for all the thoughtful feedback. It actually pushed me to dig into the existing research on Rock–Paper–Scissors, because the central question is exactly the one many of you raised: is this fundamentally a game of luck, or is there genuine skill to uncover?

There has been quite a bit of scientific research on repeated RPS over the last decade.
The consensus seems to be:

In theory, perfect play is random (the Nash equilibrium), so against a perfectly random opponent there’s nothing to exploit.
Humans, however, are consistently 
not
 random. Multiple studies show we develop predictable habits, react differently after wins and losses, and exhibit individual behavioural patterns.
Researchers have even built adaptive AIs that beat the vast majority of human participants by learning those patterns.

That doesn’t prove my game idea works. Far from it.
The real unanswered question is whether 
humans can learn to recognize and exploit those same behavioural patterns in other humans
, without AI assistance, in a way that is both skillful and fun.
I also chose five moves instead of three because I suspect it creates a richer behavioural space. It could make the game deeper… or it could simply make pattern recognition too difficult. I honestly don’t know yet.
That’s why I’m building prototypes first instead of assuming the idea works.
If the research ends up showing that skill never reliably emerges, then I’ll happily conclude the hypothesis was wrong. But at this point I think there’s enough evidence to justify investigating it.
